content: Genital herpes is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by two types of herpes simplex viruses: HSV-1 and HSV-2. HSV-1 is commonly associated with oral herpes, which can lead to cold sores or fever blisters around the mouth. However, HSV-1 can also cause genital herpes through oral-genital contact. HSV-2 is more commonly associated with genital herpes. Many individuals with oral or genital herpes may not exhibit symptoms or may have symptoms so mild that they go unnoticed or are mistaken for other skin conditions, such as pimples or ingrown hairs. When symptoms of genital herpes do occur, they often present as one or more blisters in the genital, rectal, or oral areas. These blisters eventually rupture, leaving painful sores that may take over a week to heal. The first outbreak may also be accompanied by flu-like symptoms, such as fever, body aches, or swollen lymph nodes. Recurrent outbreaks are common, particularly with HSV-2, but they tend to be less severe and shorter in duration over time. Despite being a lifelong infection, the frequency of outbreaks often decreases as time passes. Herpes can increase the risk of acquiring or transmitting HIV. The presence of herpes sores or breaks in the skin provides an entry point for HIV. Even in the absence of visible sores, herpes can increase the number of immune cells in the genital area, which are targeted by HIV. Individuals with both HIV and genital herpes are at a higher risk of transmitting HIV to an uninfected partner during sexual activity. Genital herpes is transmitted through vaginal, anal, or oral sex with an infected partner. The virus can spread through contact with herpes sores, saliva, genital fluids, or the skin of an infected partner, even if no visible sores are present. It is also possible to contract genital herpes from a partner with oral herpes through oral sex. However, herpes cannot be transmitted through casual contact with objects like toilet seats, bedding, or towels. Preventing genital herpes involves abstaining from sexual activity or engaging in a mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes. Consistent and correct use of condoms can reduce the risk of transmission, but it does not eliminate the risk entirely, as herpes can be shed from areas not covered by a condom. If a partner has genital herpes, taking daily antiviral medication and avoiding sexual activity during outbreaks can further reduce the risk of transmission. Pregnant individuals with genital herpes should inform their healthcare provider, as the infection can pose risks to the baby. Herpes can be transmitted to the baby during delivery, potentially causing neonatal herpes, a serious and potentially fatal condition. Pregnant individuals may be prescribed antiviral medication during the later stages of pregnancy to reduce the risk of an outbreak at the time of delivery. If active herpes sores are present during labor, a cesarean delivery may be recommended to prevent transmission to the baby. Diagnosis of genital herpes is typically made through clinical examination of sores or by testing a sample from the sores. In the absence of sores, a blood test can detect antibodies to HSV, indicating a past or current infection. However, blood tests cannot determine when or from whom the infection was acquired. There is no cure for genital herpes, but antiviral medications can help manage the condition. These medications can reduce the severity and duration of outbreaks, as well as lower the risk of transmitting the virus to sexual partners. Daily suppressive therapy, which involves taking antiviral medication every day, can be particularly effective in reducing the likelihood of transmission. If left untreated, genital herpes can cause painful sores and may lead to complications in individuals with weakened immune systems. Additionally, touching herpes sores or their fluids can spread the virus to other parts of the body, such as the eyes. It is important to avoid touching sores and to wash hands thoroughly if contact occurs. For pregnant individuals, untreated genital herpes can result in complications for both the parent and the baby, including the risk of neonatal herpes. While a diagnosis of genital herpes can be emotionally challenging, it is important to remember that the condition is manageable with proper medical care. Open communication with sexual partners and healthcare providers is essential for managing the infection and maintaining healthy relationships.
